headlines.title: Child's death in San Jose under investigation
headlines.description: An investigation was launched Tuesday after a child died in San Jose, according to police. Officers responded at about 1:40 p.m. to the 2500 block of Fontaine Road to investigate a report of an unresponsive child, police said. First responders tried to save the child, but the child was pronounced dead at the scene, according to police. Additional information wasn’t immediately known. “As with all major injury or death investigations involving a child, the San José Police Department is conducting an investigation per Santa Clara County protocol and is working closely with the SCC District Attorney’s Office,” police said in a statement. “Investigations into child deaths are highly detailed processes that require extensive evidence collection and thorough follow-up to determine the cause and manner of death.” Police said the investigation is active and ongoing.

headlines.title: 7 students arrested after fight at Santa Rosa high school
headlines.description: Seven students were arrested after a fight at a Santa Rosa high school prompted a campus lockdown Tuesday, with police saying a 15-year-old student displayed a knife and tried to approach another student. Santa Rosa police said they responded to Montgomery High School at 1250 Hahman Drive at about 1:10 p.m. after receiving multiple reports of a physical altercation involving students. Initial reports indicated a knife had been displayed, and some unconfirmed information suggested a firearm might also be involved. Sixteen officers responded as the campus was placed on lockdown while police searched the area, identified students and reviewed video footage. Initial information suggested the fight might be gang-related, police said. Investigators determined that a 15-year-old male student brandished a knife and aggressively advanced toward another student. A school employee stepped between them, preventing the student from advancing further. The student fled before officers arrived. Police found the student hiding behind a residence across the street on Rock Creek Drive. A large knife with a 4-inch fixed blade, believed to have been used, was recovered nearby. Several students had minor injuries and were treated at the scene. One student was taken to a hospital for injuries to the face and hand. Despite the initial reports, police found no firearm. They said they have no evidence that a gun was involved. After officers searched the campus and determined there was no ongoing threat, the lockdown was lifted shortly after 1:55 p.m. Middle school students were released to parents and guardians first, followed by high school students, with officers assisting in the process. All seven students were arrested on suspicion of battery on school grounds. They included a 14-year-old boy, three 15-year-old boys and three 16-year-old boys. One of the 15-year-olds, whom police identified as the student who possessed the knife, was also arrested on suspicion of brandishing a weapon and possessing a weapon on school grounds. Police withheld the students’ names because they are juveniles. Anyone with information about this case can contact the Santa Rosa Police Department’s Gang Crimes Team at 707-543-4021 or submit an anonymous tip at srcity.org/CrimeTips.

headlines.title: East Bay cities move to pause new AI data centers
headlines.description: East Bay cities are taking action on new AI data centers, with Hayward becoming the latest to approve a temporary moratorium on their development. The Hayward City Council approved a 45-day moratorium on the development of new AI data centers Tuesday night. The moratoriums come amid concerns that the large computing facilities are too noisy and strain the electrical grid and water systems. The city says the next month and a half will serve as a timeout for staff to monitor and analyze the impacts of the four AI data centers already in operation. Staff will also assess whether it is wise to approve two new 99-megawatt data centers proposed for the area of Arden Road and Corporate Avenue. The moratorium could be extended for two years. In Richmond Tuesday night, the City Council voted to extend its current moratorium for more than 22 months. During public comment, Richmond resident Toronto Abbott expressed concerns about data centers. “We’re on the cusp of a really terrifying era,” Abbott said. “And it’s not just that the change is different and new.” Abbott said he believes the wealth and power coming from data centers will not benefit residents and expressed concerns about the impact on jobs. On Monday, the Pittsburg City Council directed staff to draft a 45-day moratorium on AI data centers in the city. The Pittsburg City Council will consider that moratorium next Monday.

headlines.title: Man dies after shooting in Oakland
headlines.description: A man died after a shooting in Oakland early Wednesday morning, according to police. Oakland police responded shortly before 1:30 a.m. to multiple ShotSpotter activations in the 2000 block of International Boulevard. When officers arrived, they found an adult man suffering from apparent gunshot wounds. Officers attempted life-saving measures before the man was taken to a hospital, where he later died. The Oakland Police Department’s Homicide Section is investigating the circumstances surrounding the shooting. No additional information was immediately available. Anyone with information, video or photos related to the case is asked to contact OPD’s Homicide Section at 510-238-3821, the Tip Line at 510-238-7950 or email cidvideos@oaklandca.gov.

headlines.title: More Oakland residents say city is headed in right direction, survey finds
headlines.description: A new survey shows more Oakland residents believe their city is headed in the right direction, though concerns remain. According to the annual Pulse Survey released Wednesday by the Oakland Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce, more Oakland residents believe the city is headed in the right direction than the wrong direction for the first time since 2017. The findings are based on interviews with 720 Oakland residents conducted over a nine-day period that ended Sunday. 46% said Oakland is headed in the right direction, while 36% said it’s headed in the wrong direction. For comparison, in 2024, only 12% said the city was headed in the right direction, compared to the 75% that said it was headed the wrong direction. NBC Bay Area’s Bob Redell has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Thousands of California state workers walk off job in one-day strike
headlines.description: Thousands of state workers have walked off the job in a one-day strike that is expected to be felt across the Bay Area. SEIU Local 1000 puts the number of workers on strike at about 95,000. The workers serve in more than 140 state departments and agencies, including the DMV and state benefits programs such as disability and unemployment. The strike is happening statewide and for the first time in the union’s history. In the Bay Area, there are two locations where workers will be on the picket lines: outside the California Public Utilities Commission in San Francisco and at the Elihu Harris State Building in Oakland. SEIU Local 1000 is the largest public-sector union in the state and one of the largest in the country. The one-day strike comes after failed negotiations between workers and Gov. Gavin Newsom’s administration. NBC Bay Area’s Ginger Conejer Saab has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: New speed cameras installed in San Jose
headlines.description: San Jose has installed new speed cameras throughout the city to keep streets safer. Over the weekend, crews put up 33 automated speed enforcement cameras as part of a five-year pilot program authorized under a new California state law. San Jose has recorded 41 traffic deaths this year. City leaders hope the cameras will help save lives. The program has already launched in Oakland and San Francisco. In San Francisco, the city says dangerous speeding dropped by 84% at camera locations during the first 18 months of enforcement. Numbers also show that San Francisco had roughly 40,000 fewer cases of speeding every day across camera locations.

headlines.title: Netflix doesn't want investors to worry, despite recent shake-ups, layoffs
headlines.description: Following a dramatic C-suite reshuffle and its largest round of layoffs in years, Netflix’s top executives assured investors on Tuesday that they have a plan to keep audiences hooked. The streaming giant announced that its third quarter revenue grew 12% year over year to $12.9 billion, while net income rose 48%, to nearly $3.7 billion. “Our engagement is solid, and it will allow us to continue to grow as we have for the last several years,” co-CEO Greg Peters said during the streamer’s third quarter earnings call, referring to the company’s performance in the U.S. “But we know that we can do better.” The revenue increase comes amid upheaval at Netflix, which last week laid off roughly 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce, and ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria and top film executives Dan Lin and Doug Belgrad. “We believe we have a responsibility to make hard trade-offs in service of our members, our partners, our employees, our investors, and ultimately our long-term growth,” Peters said of the layoffs. “That was the simple thinking behind it, and what motivated these recent changes.” Over the last year, Netflix’s stock has dropped significantly, from a price of $124.14 in October of 2025 to $68.69 on Tuesday, due to slowing revenue growth. Netflix remains the biggest subscription streaming video service in the world, with more than 325 million global subscribers. But the company has struggled to boost user engagement amid increasing competition from YouTube, despite expanding its push into live sports, video podcasts and gaming. streaming services Oct 14 NFL May 13 Media May 11 Co-chief Ted Sarandos tapped former Disney and Fox executive Peter Rice to step into Bajaria’s role, telling investors and journalists that the Disney alum “understands talent relations.” “In a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work, and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life,” Sarandos said Tuesday. “Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world. Now, that’s a key aspect of what I believe Peter can improve on looking forward.” The changes at Netflix come as other major Hollywood studios are also trying to reduce costs and streamline operations. The Walt Disney Co. has cut hundreds of jobs this year under new CEO Josh D’Amaro, and David Ellison’s Skydance is expected to shrink its workforce across Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. (In February, Netflix officially pulled out of a deal to buy WBD, ceding in a bidding war to Paramount.) Amid industry consolidation, Netflix reported slower revenue growth in the U.S. and Canada, where sales rose 11% in the third quarter, compared with 17% a year earlier. Still, in its letter to shareholders, the streaming giant stressed that its strength lies in its “differentiated, exclusive, professionally produced series, films and live events.” It singled out the performances of recent programming, including: “The Last House,”; “Death of the Pastor’s Wife”; and an NFL game in Australia. It also touted its upcoming slate of shows and movies, such as: “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” a David Fincher-directed, Quentin Tarantino-written sequel to “Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood”; “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey,” starring Melissa McCarthy and Clive Owen; new seasons of its popular shows, “The Diplomat” and “Nobody Wants This”; three NFL games on Thanksgiving Eve and Christmas Day; and the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua fight. During the earnings call, Sarandos also discussed Netflix’s recent theatrical releases, including its first disclosure of box office results for Spanish-language Oscar contender “La bola negra,” and upcoming IMAX releases such as Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew.” “Reminder, we are a streaming first business. That is our core,” Sarandos said. “We start off by looking at the projects we have, asking ourselves how do we best serve movie lovers, many of whom are our members who want to see that movie in a theater, and how do we do it without actually harming the view value to Netflix?” Allie Canal contributed.

headlines.title: Bay Area voter guide: What to know about the November 2026 election
headlines.description: What to Know — Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026 California will choose a new governor to replace Gavin Newsom, who terms out after this year. The choices are Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton. Voters will decide 14 state propositions. Regional sales tax Measure RTM, the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, aims to increase funds for public transit. California’s Congressional District 11 race features Scott Wiener and Connie Chan competing to succeed Nancy Pelosi. Aisha Wahab and Melissa Hernandez will face off again after a special election in August where Wahab secured victory to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. All 80 California Assembly seats are up for reelection, as well as 20 Senate seats. California’s general election is Nov. 3, with statewide races and propositions as well as key local races and measures across the Bay Area. Here’s what you need to know to cast your ballot, including important dates and deadlines, how to register or check your status, where and when to vote, and what’s on the ballot. In this guide: Key election dates Check voter registration status How to register to vote How to find your polling place What to bring to your polling place How to track your mail-in ballot Why is California choosing a new governor? 14 California propositions What to watch Alameda County What to watch Contra Costa County What to watch Napa County What to watch San Francisco What to watch San Mateo County What to watch Santa Clara County What to watch Solano County County election offices Key election dates The last day to register to vote for the Nov. 3 general election is Oct. 19. County election officials will start mailing ballots by Oct. 5. Ballot drop-off locations open on Oct. 6 Last day to register to vote for the general election is Oct. 19. First vote centers open for early in-person voting in all Voter’s Choice Act counties on Oct. 24. In person early voting locations in the state open on Oct. 31. Election Day, Nov. 3, is the last day to vote in-person or return a ballot by 8 p.m. Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Vote-by-mail ballots must be postmarked no later than Nov. 3. If mailing on election day, get a hand-stamped postmark from a postal employee inside a post office. Visit the California Secretary of State’s website for a full list of key dates and deadlines. Check voter registration status Voters can check their registration at voterstatus.sos.ca.gov to confirm their mailing address and voting status. How to register to vote California residents can register to vote in elections at registertovote.ca.gov. Note Oct. 19 is the last day to register for the general election. Same day voter registration window will be open from Oct. 20 up to the Nov. 3 election day. Visit caearlyvoting.sos.ca.gov for a list of early voting locations to complete same day registration. How to find your polling place Visit the California Secretary of State’s website, where you can input your address to find your polling location and see what is on your ballot. Voters can also visit their county elections office for more information. Scroll down to the Bay Area county election offices section of this guide for further contact information. What to bring to your polling place Voters usually are not required to show identification to a polling place worker before casting a ballot, according to the Secretary of State’s website. There are some instances when providing identification is required: Voting for the first time after registering to vote by mail and did not provide a driver license number California identification number or the last four digits of social security number are missing on registration form In these cases voters should plan to bring identification to a polling place or bring a copy of it with their vote-by-mail ballot. The Secretary of State says the following are acceptable forms of identification: Passport Driver license Official state identification card Student identification card Copy of recent utility bill Sample ballot booklet received from county elections office Any document received by a government agency How to track your mail-in ballot Voters can track their vote-by-mail ballot and confirm it has been received by using the state’s Where’s My Ballot? tool at california.ballottrax.net/voter/. Ballots mailed in may take a few days to appear on the website. Why is California choosing a new governor? Gov. Gavin Newsom terms out after this year and voters will choose between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton, who both advanced to the general election after a wild primary. Becerra has served as former President Joe Biden’s top health official and oversaw the response to the coronavirus pandemic. He was also the California’s attorney general during President Donald Trump’s first term and has more than two decades of experience as a congressmember. Hilton was a conservative commentator with a show on Fox News for six years. He also worked as an adviser to former British prime minister David Cameron. What are the 14 California propositions voters will decide in the November election? Here’s a list of the California propositions on the November ballot. Use the expandable graphic below for a breakdown on what to know about each measure. 2026 California Ballot Propositions Click on a proposition to see more information about what will happen if it does or doesn’t pass. Source: NBC Staff Reports • Interactive: Annetta Stogniew Regional measure to watch Measure RTM: The Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative, is a regional sales tax aimed at increasing funds for public transit. It includes 5 Bay Area counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, San Francisco, San Mateo, and Santa Clara. Races and measures to watch in Alameda County California Congressional District 14: California lawmaker Aisha Wahab and Bay Area Rapid Transit Director Melissa Hernandez will face off again to determine who will serve the next full two-year term. Wahab topped Hernandez in an August special election to serve the remainder of former California U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell’s term. Swalwell resigned from Congress earlier this year after sexual assault and misconduct allegations. District 14 includes the East Bay cities such as Fremont, Hayward and Livermore. Measure X in Berkeley: Would establish 10% limit on annual rent increases and other changes to the city’s rent ordinance. Measure Y in Berkeley: Parcel tax to pay for arts projects. Measure Z in Berkeley: Parcel tax to fund a public bank. Measure AA in Berkeley: Increase soda tax Measure EE in Oakland: Shift city to a strong mayor system. Measure FF in Oakland: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Alameda County and additional election information, visit the Alameda County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Contra Costa County In Contra Costa County, several county board of education seats are open. In Richmond, residents will vote on a new mayor while voters in San Pablo will weigh in on Measure S, which would limit rent increases. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Contra Costa County and additional election information, visit the Contra Costa County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Francisco San Francisco voters will weigh in on several open seats on the county board of supervisors and board of education. Proposition A: Give mayor more power to hire and fire department heads. Proposition B: Pave way for public bank. Proposition C: Increase the city’s annual contribution to an affordable housing trust fund. Proposition D: New barriers to placing measures on the ballot. Proposition E: Changes to city contracting. Proposition G: Reopen parts of the Great Highway to vehicle traffic on weekdays. Proposition H: Parcel tax to fund Muni. Proposition J: Eliminate foreclosure exemption from property transfer tax California Congressional District 11: Scott Wiener and Connie Chan compete to succeed Nancy Pelosi. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Francisco and additional election information, visit the San Francisco Department of Elections website. Races and measures to watch in San Mateo County Measure E in Redwood City: Limit rent increases. Measure Q in Half Moon Bay: Referendum to block proposed farmworker housing. Measure U in San Mateo County: Create independent commission to draw supervisor districts. For a complete list of San Mateo County measures and races on the ballot, visit smacre.gov/elections. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in San Mateo County and additional election information, visit the San Mateo County Elections website. Races and measures to watch in Santa Clara County In San Jose, incumbents Peter Ortiz and Bien Doan are up for re-election in Districts 5 and 7, respectively, and there’s an open seat in District 9. Races and measures to watch in Solano County Solano County Board of Supervisors, District 4: Mike Silva and John Carli face in a runoff in a district covering Vacaville and Dixon. Measure E in Solano County: New tax on data centers and battery storage facilities in the unincorporated county areas. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Solano County and additional election information, visit the Solano County Registrar of Voters website. Races and measures to watch in Sonoma County California Congressional District 1: Mike McGuire will face James Gallagher in a seat redistricted by Proposition 50. California Congressional District 4: Mike Thompson faces Eric Jones. State Assembly District 12: Eric Lucan and Jackie Elward compete in a battle between business and labor. 🗳️ For a complete list of races and measures on the ballot in Sonoma County and additional election information, visit the Sonoma County Registrar of Voters website. headlines.title: Indiana man pleads guilty in 2008 rape case in San Jose
headlines.description: An 18-year-old rape case in San Jose has come to a close after officials said a man from Indiana pleaded guilty. In 2008, James Whisenand broke into an elderly woman’s apartment in the Willow Glen neighborhood, punched her in the face and raped her, according to police. Investigators didn’t have a suspect until 2024, when a crime lab matched DNA from the case to another sexual assault case in Indiana, prompting Whisenand’s arrest. The victim died of natural causes in 2011. “Years and distance do not matter,” Santa Clara County District Attorney Jeff Rosen said in a statement. “This Office will never stop seeking justice for the people who have been hurt in our community. I just wish I could have told her that we got him. I wish she was here with us today.”

headlines.title: Brush fire spreads to home in the Oakland Hills
headlines.description: A small brush fire spread to one home in the Oakland Hills Tuesday before firefighters were able to stop its forward progress. The Oakland Fire Department (OFD) said the blaze broke out at about 11:45 a.m. along the 1000 block of Panoramic Way, located above the UC Berkeley campus. Forward progress was stopped by about 1:15 p.m. Flames burned through vegetation on a hillside before spreading to the roof and siding of a home along Panoramic Way, according to the fire department. More than 70 firefighters from multiple jurisdictions responded to the scene, ultimately stopping the fire at roughly an acre and a half. “Crews did a fantastic job,” OFD Chief Damon Covington said. “This had potential to take off and be a large-scale event. The multi-jurisdiction response was seamless.” No evacuation orders were issued, but residents on Panoramic Way were asked to temporarily shelter in place. No injuries were reported. The cause of the fire wasn’t immediately known.

headlines.title: ‘We want ICE out': Advocates rally after immigration agents detain man in San Francisco
headlines.description: People packed the steps of San Francisco City Hall Tuesday to denounce what they called a dangerous detention by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on city streets. Security camera footage of Monday’s detention showed three people – one wearing a plaid shirt and holding a gun along with two uniformed and masked ICE officers – approach a man on a sidewalk. One of the agents could be heard asking the man why he was running. The man responded by saying it was because he didn’t know them. The agents then took the man into custody as he repeatedly shouted, “I’m a U.S. citizen.” According to the San Francisco Public Defender’s Office, the man who was detained is their client, but officials wouldn’t share details about why agents may have detained him or if they have made contact with him since he was detained. “We’re still trying to figure out what’s going on in the case,” Deputy Public Defender Francisco Ugarte said. “The issue isn’t this one person. The issue is around the way ICE is making arrests.” During Tuesday’s rally at city hall, Ugarte did not elaborate on questions about a statement ICE released to media outlets about the man who was detained. In that statement, ICE claims the man they arrested, 51-year-old Milton Ramos-Ramirez of El Salvador, has a conviction for voluntary manslaughter in California and may have ties to the Sureños street gang. At the rally, supervisors pledged to quickly pass a supplemental funding measure to go to immigration rapid response teams in the city. “We are here today because it has come to our front door,” Supervisor Jackie Fielder said. “We are here today because in San Francisco, we do not stand for hate. We are here because we want ICE out of San Francisco.”
